title: ARIA head says 'very little' is known about proposed AI carveout
transcript:
Host: A parliamentary inquiry into artificial intelligence is due to hand down its final report this week. It comes as music artists maintain pressure on the government to protect their work from being used to train large language models without compensation. Amid reports the government is designing an opt out function for musicians. Last week, Australian musicians rallied against AI theft at the ARIA Awards in Sydney with a global superstar adding his pre-recorded voice to the mix.
Superstar: I want to send an important message to the Australian government. You have a duty to protect Australian artists and their work. Don't let AI use any Australian artist work without full permission.
Host: That's Elton John speaking at last week's ARIA Awards. Well, Annabelle Hurd is chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association and joins me now. Annabelle, welcome to the program.
Annabelle Hurd: Good morning.
Host: How would you describe the strength of feeling on this issue amongst musicians right now?
Annabelle Hurd: Uh, look, I think it was pretty evident on Wednesday last week what the strength of feeling um on this issue was, um, and of course it's not just musicians either, it's authors, it's um photographers, it's everybody who relies on copyright basically to make a living.
Host: What do we know about this proposed AI carve out?
Annabelle Hurd: Uh very little. Um all we know really is what we saw reported in um an article last week. Um I'm not sure how you can carve any type of copyright work out. Um but at the end of the day, every copyright owner deserves the basic right of being asked permission before their work is used for any use that comes within copyright rights, but AI training is definitely one of those. So that's what the campaign's all about.
Host: Music, film and television often overlap. How would something like a carve out theoretically work, and is it even possible for one industry to opt out without directly affecting other creative sectors?
Annabelle Hurd: Yeah, look, I think even, you know, the fact that we're talking about an opt out is kind of ridiculous in the first place. Um, our copyright law works perfectly well in this country. If the AI companies that have trained on our content have trained on that content in Australia, we would be able to sue them at the moment under existing copyright law. That's what's happening in the US at the moment. 
      Um, if we go down a path around training schemes and opt outs and all the rest of it, then we're not going to be able to do that in this country. So, you know, we're standing with the rest of the creative industry, sorry, the rest of the creative industries, um, because you're right, it is extremely difficult to differentiate content, um, and, you know, enforce our rights when you've got a scheme um that allows companies to train on your content without permission.
Host: Many artists don't actually hold the full rights to their music. It's the agency's they're signed to. Would talent in those circumstances have any rights on whether labels can choose to feed music into AI training models?
Annabelle Hurd: Well, there are many artists that do own their copyright. Um, so that's the first thing I would say. Secondly, the deals that have been done with music companies and AI companies so far, and there are several. It's a, it's a very early developing market, but it is certainly a developing market, have revolted around an opt-in for artists. 
      So, it's very important that everyone has the right to opt-in to training here. Um, but of course, you know, copyright is the foundation that everybody in the ecosystem gets paid and relies on, you know, to generate an income. So, no matter who owns the copyright, it still supports the entire creative ecosystem because without it, there is no economic value in our work at all.
Host: You're listening to Radio National Breakfast and I'm speaking to Annabelle Hurd, Ari's chief executive. Last week's ARIA Awards were were filled with anti-AI messaging, some of it directed at the current government with slogans like not AIs to take, which your organization is pushing. Has anyone from the Albanese government reached out to you since the award ceremony?
Annabelle Hurd: No.
Host: What do you think about that?
Annabelle Hurd: Uh, well, look, I know at the moment there's lots being discussed. We've got this committee report coming this week. Um, there are proposals supposedly under consideration and we've seen some versions of those. Um, we haven't seen anything with an opt out in it. 
      Um, there's no one, you know, in the music industry that, you know, that has been involved in this debate that is anti-AI as a concept, or I mean, there are, but you know, the music industry is certainly open to doing deals and to talking to AI companies and to exploring, you know, what AI can mean for for artists, for consumers, for our businesses. 
      Um, so we're certainly open to a conversation with those companies about using our work. Some artists don't want to have a bar of it, and that should be their right to say no, we don't want to we're not interested in participating. But, yeah, we don't know what's going on.
Host: The development of AIs is moving very, very quickly. What ultimately is the solution here in your view?
Annabelle Hurd: Well, the solution is the existing framework that we have for copyright, that copyright is not a barrier to AI training in this country. And countries around the world have been approached by these companies to change their laws to enable the copyright carve out and they've said no. The UK said no, Canada said no, Brazil said no, many other countries, Hong Kong, India, both said no recently. 
      And I'm not sure why we're having this conversation when Australia is probably one of the most attractive countries in the world for AI companies to come and train and to set up businesses. In fact, they have done so. And both Anthropic and OpenAI have said that no matter what Australia does on copyright, they will provide us with access to their training models for national security purposes, they're invested here, they're committed to Australia. 
      So, I'm not sure why we're still having this conversation about a carve out for copyright.
Host: What needs to happen now, do you think?
Annabelle Hurd: Well, I mean, we're spending so much time and resource um across the creative industries trying to establish what's happening and where this issue is going. Um, we really need um the government and others involved in this conversation to to tell us what's happening. 
      Um, but basically, they need to shut the door to these companies and say, we're not going to give you a a commercial um a commercially advantageous outcome, sorry, a commercially advantageous outcome. 
      We're not going to change our copyright law to give in to you. And that will enable these companies to actually come to us and discuss deals. But that needs to happen and it needs to happen soon.
Host: Annabelle Hurd, thank you for joining me this morning.
Annabelle Hurd: Thank you so much.
